entry: American animator, filmmaker, songwriter and actor. Parker studied film and Japanese at the University of Colorado Boulder, where he met his creative partner [[Matt Stone]]. Together they created the animated satire [[South Park|*South Park*]] and made its feature film *South Park: Bigger, Longer & Uncut* (1999). Parker's satirical action film *Team America: World Police* (2004) used marionettes. With Robert Lopez he cowrote the musical *The Book of Mormon*, which won four Tony Awards and a Grammy. Parker has received five Primetime Emmy Awards and a Peabody for *South Park*, and an Academy Award nomination for the song "Blame Canada."

Formal legal proceeding in which parties to a dispute present [[Evidence (law)|evidence]] before a tribunal, a body with authority to adjudicate claims. The tribunal, which may be a [[Court|court]], may be presided over by a [[Judge|judge]], a [[Jury|jury]] or another designated trier of fact, and aims to resolve the dispute. A trial before a community jury is a jury trial; one held solely before a judge is a bench trial. Criminal trials resolve accusations, usually brought by a government, against a person accused of a [[Crime|crime]], and defendants' rights are typically broad because the state seeks to deprive them of life, liberty or property. Civil trials settle lawsuits and other non-criminal disputes. In [[Common law|common law]] systems an adversarial approach is used, with a judge as neutral referee; there is a [[Presumption of innocence|presumption of innocence]] and the burden of proof lies on the prosecution. [[Appeal|Appeals]] are generally not considered trials, because they review evidence from the trial court without admitting new evidence.

Fire at a garment factory in Greenwich Village, [[Manhattan]], on March 25, 1911. It killed 146 garment workers, most of them recent Italian and Jewish immigrants aged 14 to 23, and was the deadliest industrial disaster in [[New York City]] history. Stairwell and exit doors were locked, a common practice meant to deter theft and unauthorized breaks, and many workers jumped from high windows. The building had no sprinklers. The fire led to legislation requiring improved factory safety standards and helped spur growth of the International Ladies' Garment Workers' Union.

Figurate number counting the dots in an equilateral triangle. The nth triangular number is the sum of the integers 1 through n, equal to n(n+1)/2, giving the sequence 1, 3, 6, 10, 15, 21. The formula may originate with the Pythagoreans in the 5th century BC and was described by the Irish monk Dicuil in about 816. An apocryphal story credits [[Carl Friedrich Gauss|Gauss]] with finding the relationship as a youth. Proof is by [[Mathematical induction|induction]], and computing large triangular numbers can overflow an integer before the final [[Division (mathematics)|division]] by 2.

Spiral galaxy 2.878 million [[Light-year|light-years]] from Earth, in the constellation Triangulum. Also designated Messier 33 (M33) or NGC 598, it is the third-largest member of the [[Local Group]], after the [[Andromeda Galaxy]] and the [[Milky Way]], with a D25 isophotal diameter of 18.74 kiloparsecs (61,120 light-years). It is the second-smallest spiral galaxy in the Local Group, after the [[Large Magellanic Cloud]], and is believed to be a satellite of the Andromeda Galaxy or to be rebounding into it. To some observers with fully dark-adapted eyes it is the farthest permanent entity visible without magnification. The Italian astronomer Giovanni Battista Hodierna probably discovered it before 1654. Charles Messier cataloged it independently on August 25–26, 1764, and [[William Herschel]] in 1784. Its brightest [[H II region]], NGC 604, was cataloged separately.

First and shortest period of the Mesozoic Era, from 251.902 to 201.4 million years ago. It began after the [[Permian–Triassic extinction event]] and ended with the [[Triassic–Jurassic extinction]]. Its three epochs are Early, Middle and Late Triassic. [[Reptile|Reptiles]], especially archosaurs, were the chief land vertebrates; the first [[Dinosaur|dinosaurs]] appeared in the Late Triassic but did not dominate until the [[Jurassic]]. Some archosaurs became the [[Pterosaur|pterosaurs]], the first vertebrates to fly, and the first stem-group [[Mammal|mammals]] appeared and survived the extinction event. The supercontinent [[Pangaea]] dominated the globe but began splitting into Laurasia and Gondwana in the latest Triassic. The climate was mostly hot and dry, with deserts across Pangaea's interior. The name, from Greek *triás* ('triad'), was coined in 1834 by Friedrich Alberti for three rock layers in southern Germany.

Mass extinction at the boundary of the Triassic and Jurassic periods, 201.4 million years ago. It was one of five major extinction events of the Phanerozoic. About 23–34% of marine genera disappeared; [[Coral|corals]], bivalves, brachiopods, bryozoans and radiolarians suffered severe losses, and conodonts were wiped out. On land, all archosauromorph reptiles other than crocodylomorphs, [[Dinosaur|dinosaurs]] and [[Pterosaur|pterosaurs]] became extinct, while crocodylomorphs, dinosaurs, pterosaurs and mammals were largely untouched and dominated land for the next 135 million years. The cause is generally considered to be volcanic eruptions in the Central Atlantic magmatic province, which released [[Carbon dioxide|carbon dioxide]] and toxic [[Mercury (element)|mercury]], causing global warming and ocean acidification. Older hypotheses proposed gradual climate and sea-level change or [[Asteroid|asteroid]] strikes.

Sexual practice between women involving vulva-to-vulva contact or rubbing the vulva against a partner's body, especially to stimulate the clitoris. Also called tribbing, it is analogous to *frot*, penis-to-penis contact. In ancient Greek and Roman sexuality, a *tribas* was a woman or intersex person who penetrated a partner using the clitoris or a dildo. The term also reflected beliefs about women's capability as penetrative partners, and those accused of penetrative sex faced ridicule or punishment. In the 18th century it was used in pornographic libels against [[Marie Antoinette]]. Modern usage typically refers to non-penetrative sex between women.

Human social group larger than a lineage or [[Clan|clan]] but smaller than a chiefdom, [[Ethnicity|ethnicity]], nation or state. The term is used most in [[Anthropology|anthropology]], where its definition is contested because of differing theories of [[Kinship|kinship]] and the difficulty of applying one concept to very diverse societies. Membership may rest on kinship, ethnicity, language, dwelling place, political group, religion or oral tradition. Anthropologist Elman Service classified societies as egalitarian [[Hunter-gatherer|hunter-gatherer]] bands, tribal societies with limited rank, stratified tribal societies led by chieftains, and [[Civilization|civilizations]] with complex hierarchies. Morton Fried argued in 1967 that bands organized into tribes to resist the violence and exploitation of early kingdoms and states. In the United States, Native American tribes have "domestic dependent nation" status and a government-to-government relationship with the federal government.

Genus of large chasmosaurine [[Dinosaur|dinosaur]] of the Late [[Cretaceous]] period, about 69 to 66 million years ago, in what is now western North America. Its name means "three-horned face" in Greek, for its three skull horns. With a bony frill and a four-legged body, it was one of the largest and best-known ceratopsians, measuring 8–9 m (26–30 ft) long and weighing up to 6–10 t. It was one of the last non-avian dinosaurs, living until the [[Cretaceous–Paleogene extinction event]]. It shared its range with [[Tyrannosaurus]], which most likely preyed on it. The frill and horns were long viewed as defenses against predators, but more recent interpretations favor species identification, courtship and dominance display. Two species, *T. horridus* and *T. prorsus*, are considered valid, although 17 have been named.

Halloween custom in which costumed children and adults go door to door asking for treats with the phrase "trick or treat." The "treat" is usually candy, or money in some cultures, and the "trick" is an idle threat of mischief if none is given. Its roots lie in guising, performing for food at Halloween, recorded in Scotland and Ireland from at least the 16th century. The earliest known North American guising was in [[British Columbia]], [[Canada]], in 1898, and the phrase was first recorded in [[Ontario]] in 1917. In Mexico, children ask for a calaverita, a small sugar or chocolate skull.

Seaport in northeastern [[Italy|Italy]], capital of the Friuli-Venezia Giulia region, at the head of the Gulf of Trieste on the [[Adriatic Sea|Adriatic]]. A prosperous trading hub under the [[Habsburg monarchy]] from 1382 until 1918, it became the fourth largest city of the Austro-Hungarian Empire, after [[Vienna]], Budapest and Prague. After [[World War II|World War II]] it became the Free Territory of Trieste, a major site of struggle between the Eastern and Western blocs. Today it is a deep-water port considered the end point of the maritime [[Silk Road]], and it hosts many international organizations and research institutions.

Real-valued functions of an [[Angle|angle]], defined as ratios of two side lengths of a right triangle. The most common are sine, cosine and tangent, with reciprocals cosecant, secant and cotangent. Each has an inverse function and an analog among the [[Hyperbolic functions|hyperbolic functions]]. They are used in all sciences related to geometry, such as [[Navigation|navigation]], solid mechanics, celestial mechanics and [[Geodesy|geodesy]], and they are among the simplest periodic functions, widely used for studying periodic phenomena through [[Fourier analysis|Fourier analysis]]. Early definitions applied only to acute angles; the standard [[Unit circle|unit circle]] extends sine and cosine to the whole real line, and modern definitions use infinite series or differential equations to extend them to the complex plane. A superscript −1 denotes the inverse function, so sin⁻¹x means arcsin x, not a reciprocal.

Class of extinct marine [[Arthropod|arthropods]], named for their three-lobed body. Trilobites were among the most successful early animals, existing in oceans for almost 270 million years, with more than 22,000 species described. Their mineralized exoskeletons, made of [[Calcite|calcite]], left an extensive fossil record that contributed to biostratigraphy, paleontology and [[Plate tectonics|plate tectonics]]. They first appear about 521 million years ago, in the [[Cambrian|Early Cambrian]], and diversity peaked in the Late Cambrian and [[Ordovician]]. Several [[Devonian]] extinctions reduced them sharply, and the last trilobites disappeared in the end-[[Permian]] mass extinction about 251.9 million years ago. They filled many niches as predators, scavengers, filter feeders and swimmers that fed on [[Plankton|plankton]]; some crawled onto land. The largest exceeded 70 centimeters (28 in) in length.

Archipelagic republic and southernmost country in the [[Caribbean]], off the northeast coast of [[Venezuela]]. Its capital is [[Port of Spain]]. [[Christopher Columbus]] first sighted Trinidad in 1498, and Spain ruled it until a British fleet took it in 1797. Both islands were ceded to Britain in 1802, unified in 1889, and became independent in 1962, when Trinidad and Tobago became a republic in 1976. Unlike most Caribbean states, the economy is primarily industrial, based on large oil and gas reserves, and the islands see fewer hurricanes because they lie farther south. Their African and Indian cultures are reflected in Carnival, Diwali and Hosay celebrations, and the islands are the birthplace of the steelpan, the limbo, calypso and soca.

Christian doctrine concerning the nature of God, holding that one God exists as three divine persons: God the Father, God the Son (Jesus Christ) and God the Holy Spirit. The persons are considered coeternal and consubstantial, sharing one essence. Early Christians developed the doctrine from the late 2nd century AD onward. It was firmly established by the 4th century through the [[First Council of Nicaea]] and became part of the [[Creed|creed]]. Most major [[Christian denomination|Christian denominations]] are Trinitarian. Nontrinitarian positions include [[Unitarianism]], binitarianism and modalism. Some [[Old Testament]] passages, such as the plural pronouns in Genesis 1:26–27, have been read as Trinitarian, though most Biblical scholars take them to refer to a heavenly court.

First detonation of a [[Nuclear weapon|nuclear weapon]], conducted by the U.S. Army on July 16, 1945, in the Jornada del Muerto desert about 35 miles (56 km) southeast of Socorro, New Mexico. Part of the [[Manhattan Project]], it tested a plutonium implosion bomb, the same design as the Fat Man bomb later dropped on Nagasaki. The code name was assigned by [[J. Robert Oppenheimer]], possibly after the poetry of [[John Donne]]. The yield was 25 kilotons of TNT (± 2 kilotons), and the test was conducted without evacuating nearby residents. Observers included [[Enrico Fermi]], [[Hans Bethe]], [[Richard Feynman]] and [[Edward Teller]].

Temperature and pressure at which a substance's gas, liquid and solid phases coexist in thermodynamic equilibrium. It is where the sublimation, fusion and vaporization curves meet on a [[Phase diagram|phase diagram]]. The triple point of [[Mercury (element)|mercury]] is at −38.8 °C (−37.8 °F) and 0.165 mPa. Helium-4 has no sublimation curve and so no triple point where its solid meets its gas. The term was first used on August 3, 1871, by James Thomson, brother of [[Lord Kelvin]]. Triple points of several substances define points on the ITS-90 temperature scale, from hydrogen (13.8033 K) to water (273.16 K, 0.01 °C). Before 2019 the triple point of water defined the [[Kelvin|kelvin]]; under the [[International System of Units]] it is now an experimentally measured constant of about 273.16 K and a vapor pressure of 611.657 pascals.

Capital and largest city of [[Libya]], on a rocky point projecting into the [[Mediterranean Sea]] on the northwest coast. Its population was about 3.246 million in 2021. [[Phoenicia|Phoenicians]] founded the city in the 7th century BC, naming it Oyat, and Greek rulers of Cyrenaica later held it as Oea. Under the Romans the region became Tripolitania, meaning "region of the three cities," named for Oea, Sabratha and Leptis Magna. Because the city has been continuously inhabited, many Roman remains lie buried, though the Arch of [[Marcus Aurelius]], from the 2nd century AD, is among the few visible. Tripoli is the country's largest commercial and manufacturing center and the site of the University of Tripoli.

State in northeastern [[India|India]], bordered by [[Assam]] and [[Mizoram]] to the east and by [[Bangladesh]] to the north, south and west. The third-smallest state, it covers 10,491 sq km and has about 3.67 million people, with a Bengali majority alongside 19 tribal communities. Agartala is the capital. Forests cover more than half the area, and Tripura has the highest number of [[Primate|primate]] species of any Indian state. Once a princely state under the [[British Raj]], it acceded to India in 1947 and became a full state in 1972.

Indian actress known for Tamil and Telugu cinema, and one of the highest-paid actresses in India. After winning the 1999 [[Chennai|Miss Chennai]] pageant she entered films, and she had her first lead in *Mounam Pesiyadhe* (2002). She rose to fame with *Saamy* (2003) and *Ghilli* (2004), and has been a leading actress in Tamil cinema for over two decades, often called the "Queen of South India." She has won five Filmfare Awards South, a Tamil Nadu State Film Award and a Nandi Award. Her highest-grossing release is the action thriller *Leo* (2023).

Romanian-French avant-garde poet, essayist and performance artist, and a founder of [[Dada]]. Born Samuel Rosenstock, he performed at the Cabaret Voltaire in [[Zurich]] during World War I, and his nihilistic poetry and manifestos became a main feature of early Dadaism. After moving to Paris in 1919 he joined the staff of the magazine *Littérature*, a step toward [[Surrealism]], and was involved in the polemics that split the movement. He later aligned himself with André Breton's Surrealism and wrote the utopian poem "The Approximate Man." Combining anti-fascism with communism, he joined the Republicans in the [[Spanish Civil War]], the French Resistance and protests against French actions in the [[Algerian War]]. He is credited with linking [[Cubism]] and [[Futurism]] to later movements, including Situationism and currents in rock music.

Remote group of volcanic islands in the South Atlantic Ocean, part of the British Overseas Territory of Saint Helena, Ascension and Tristan da Cunha. The inhabited main island, roughly 11 kilometers across, had 222 permanent inhabitants as of September 2026, all of them British Overseas Territories citizens. It has no airstrip and is a six-day journey by ship from [[Cape Town]], South Africa, and is considered the most remote inhabited place in the world. The first undisputed landing was made in 1643 by the Dutch East India Company. Gough Island, a wildlife reserve, is a [[UNESCO|UNESCO]] [[World Heritage Site|World Heritage Site]].

Music drama in three acts by [[Richard Wagner]], premiered in Munich on June 10, 1865, with Hans von Bülow conducting. Loosely based on Gottfried von Strassburg's medieval 12th-century romance *Tristan and Iseult*, it was composed from 1857 to 1859. Wagner preferred the term *Handlung* ("action") for its continuous flow, or "endless melody," in contrast to conventional opera of recitatives and showpiece arias. Its concern with striving and love beyond death was inspired in part by the philosophy of [[Arthur Schopenhauer]]. The prelude opens with the Tristan chord, whose unprecedented chromaticism and tonal ambiguity marked a turning point in the evolution of Western music. The harmony initially divided audiences, but the opera became enormously influential, directly inspiring [[Gustav Mahler]], [[Richard Strauss]] and [[Benjamin Britten]].

Radioactive [[Hydrogen|hydrogen]] isotope with one proton and two neutrons, half-life 12.32 years. Also called hydrogen-3, it is rare on Earth, formed in the atmosphere by cosmic rays and produced in nuclear reactors by irradiating [[Lithium|lithium]]. It decays by [[Beta decay|beta]] emission into [[Helium-3]], releasing 18.6 keV. Tritium powers self-illuminating lights in watches and firearm night sights, serves as a tracer in medical and scientific work, and fuels [[Nuclear fusion|fusion]] reactors with [[Deuterium]]. It is a component of hydrogen bombs. [[Ernest Rutherford]] and colleagues first detected it in 1934.
